# 

# 1\. LAB OVERVIEW

## 1.1  Why This Lab Exists

A dashboard is a tool for a decision, not a collection of graphs. Good operational dashboards answer one question for one audience: an executive wants to know whether customers are affected and the objective is met; an on-call engineer wants to know which part of the shop is unhealthy; a service owner wants the four golden signals — latency, traffic, errors, saturation — of one service. Arranged as a hierarchy (L1 executive → L2 operations → L3 service), each level links to the next, so people start at the top and drill down only where something is red.  
In this lab you audit the existing Shop Overview dashboard against design principles, publish a Golden Signals dashboard with a service variable and build its saturation panel yourself, apply the audit findings to a copy of the operational dashboard, and publish an executive summary — then connect the three levels with folders, tags and links.

| 🎯  NIIT iRUN Alignment |
| :---- |
| INCIDENT OWNERSHIP: Your dashboards show "is it bad, where, and since when" within five seconds. |
|  |
| TROUBLESHOOTING EXCELLENCE: The hierarchy takes you from a red executive tile to the failing service in two clicks. |
|  |
| OPERATIONAL READINESS: Each dashboard has an audience, a description, consistent units and thresholds, and a runbook link. |

## 1.3  Conceptual Foundation

Each level of the hierarchy has its own audience, question and design. Links connect the levels.  
*Figure: Dashboard Hierarchy — L1 Executive (availability, error budget, orders) → L2 Operations (whole shop: golden signals per route, saturation) → L3 Service (golden signals of one selected service) → Explore / Traces / Logs; "Down" and "Up" Links Keep Time Range and Variables*

| Level | Audience | Question It Answers | Design |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| L1 Executive | Management, product owners | Are customers affected? Is the objective met? | 4–6 large stats, long range, few colours, no technical terms |
| L2 Operations | On-call, incident commander | Which part of the system is unhealthy, since when? | Golden signals per area, trends, thresholds, links to L3 |
| L3 Service | Service owner, responder | What are the golden signals of this service? | Service variable, latency/traffic/errors/saturation rows |
| L4 Explore | Responder during diagnosis | Why — which request, log line, span? | Ad hoc queries, traces, logs — not a fixed dashboard |

*Figure: Information Layout — Most Important Signal Top Left; Summary Stats in the First Row (5-Second Test), Trends Below, Details Last; Same Order of Signals (Latency, Traffic, Errors, Saturation) on Every Dashboard*

## 1.4  Learning Objectives

* Audit a dashboard against design principles (audience, layout, units, thresholds, descriptions)  
* Build a Golden Signals dashboard for a selected service with a service variable  
* Add a saturation panel with correct unit, thresholds and description  
* Modify an existing operational dashboard to apply the audit findings  
* Create an executive dashboard that answers business questions  
* Organise dashboards into a hierarchy with folders, tags and links

## 1.5  What You Will NOT Do

| 🚫  Hard Stops — Absolute Prohibitions for This Lab |
| :---- |
| ✗  NEVER edit the provisioned Shop Overview directly — save a copy |
| ✗  NEVER put more than one audience on one dashboard |
| ✗  NEVER show a number without a unit and, where it matters, a threshold |
| ✗  NEVER use red and green for anything other than bad and good |
| ✗  NEVER leave the db-pool fault on after the test |

# 3\. CONCEPT DEEP-DIVE BEFORE STARTING

## 3.1  Design for One Audience and One Question

Start every dashboard with a sentence: "This dashboard tells \<audience\> whether \<question\>." Then put the answer in the first row — a few large stats with units and thresholds — so that the five-second test passes: anyone can say "good" or "bad" at a glance. Trends follow in the second row, details and breakdowns below. Keep the order of the signals the same everywhere (latency, traffic, errors, saturation), use the same colours for the same meaning, write a description on every panel (the ⓘ icon) and link to the next level down and to the runbook.

| 💡  Why This Matters Operationally |
| :---- |
| At 3 a.m. nobody reads a dashboard — they scan it. A consistent layout and clear thresholds turn scanning into a decision; an unclear dashboard sends the responder to Explore without a starting point. |
|  |
| A hierarchy reduces the number of dashboards people must know to one: the L1 or L2 entry page. Everything else is reached by links that keep the time range and variables. |

## 3.2  The Critical Distinction: Operational vs Executive Dashboards

An operational dashboard shows the current state and short trends (last 30–60 minutes, refresh 30 s) in technical units — requests per second, p95 seconds, 5xx ratio, pool utilisation — so responders can act. An executive dashboard summarises a longer period (a day, a week) against objectives in business terms — availability, error budget, completed orders — and changes slowly. Mixing them produces a page that is too technical for management and too coarse for on-call.

| ⚠️  Most Common Mistake With Dashboards |
| :---- |
| A team adds every new graph to the same dashboard. After a year it has 60 panels, three audiences and no clear first row; during incidents everyone opens Explore instead. |
|  |
| REASON: Dashboards grow by addition, never by design; nobody owns the question the page should answer. |
|  |
| YOU MUST give each dashboard an audience, a question and an owner, keep the first row to the answer, and move details to a lower level. |

## 3.3  Dashboard Design Checklist

| Principle | Check | Good Example | Bad Example |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Purpose | Title and description name audience and question | "Shop — Golden Signals" (L3) | "Shop stuff v2" |
| Layout | Answer in the first row, top left most important | p95 · traffic · errors · saturation stats | Most important graph at the bottom |
| Units & thresholds | Every number has a unit; bad is visible | p95 0.24 s, orange 0.5 s, red 1 s | "0.0712" without unit |
| Navigation | Links to next level and runbook; variables carried | "Down: Golden Signals" with includeVars | Copy-pasted dashboards per service |

| 📝  How to Decide Which Level a Panel Belongs To |
| :---- |
| Ask: "Who acts on this number, and how fast?" If management acts on it over days, it belongs on L1. If on-call acts on it in minutes for the whole system, it belongs on L2. If a service owner acts on it for one service, it belongs on L3 with a service variable. If nobody acts on it, it belongs in Explore — not on a dashboard. |

Answer: For the lab responder, ShopSim only emits metrics under env="lab", so opening the dashboard shows empty/no-data panels (N/A) until the variable is manually switched. For a real on-call responder at 3 a.m., defaulting to prod without clear visual context can cause confusion if they are investigating a staging/non-prod alert (or vice versa), wasting critical triage time or leading to false conclusions about production health.   |

| TASK 2 — GOLDEN SIGNALS (L3): Service Variable and the Saturation Signal |
| :---- |

| 2 | Build a Golden Signal Dashboard for a Selected Service*Operational Dashboard Design SOP — Day 5 — Lab 4* | ⏱ 8 min |
| :---: | :---- | :---: |

dashboards.py writes the Golden Signals dashboard with env, service and route variables and three of the four signals as stats and trends. You create the hierarchy folders, publish it, then build the fourth signal — saturation — yourself in the UI, select the checkout service and test the dashboard with the db-pool fault.

| ⌨  Task 2 — Generate and publish |
| :---- |
| ![][image6] |
| cat \> dashboards.py \<\<'EOF' |
| \#\!/usr/bin/env python3 |
| """Day 5 Lab 4 — writes two Grafana dashboards as API payloads: |
|   golden-signals.json  "Shop — Golden Signals" (L3, one selected service; the Saturation row is left for you to build) |
|   executive.json       "Shop — Executive Summary" (L1, business view of the whole shop for the selected time range)""" |
| import json |
|  |
| DS \= {"type": "prometheus", "uid": "prometheus"} |
| SEL \= 'env="\$env",service="\$service",route=\~"\$route"' |
| REQ, BKT \= "http\_server\_requests\_total", "http\_server\_request\_duration\_seconds\_bucket" |
|  |
| def thresholds(\*steps): |
|     return {"mode": "absolute", "steps": \[{"color": c, "value": v} for c, v in steps\]} |
| def panel(pid, kind, title, desc, x, y, w, h, exprs, unit, th=None, legend=None, extra=None): |
|     p \= {"id": pid, "type": kind, "title": title, "description": desc, "datasource": DS, |
|          "gridPos": {"x": x, "y": y, "w": w, "h": h}, |
|          "targets": \[{"refId": chr(65 \+ i), "datasource": DS, "expr": e, "legendFormat": (legend or \["\_\_auto"\] \* 9)\[i\]} for i, e in enumerate(exprs)\], |
|          "fieldConfig": {"defaults": {"unit": unit}, "overrides": \[\]}, "options": {}} |
|     if th: p\["fieldConfig"\]\["defaults"\]\["thresholds"\] \= th |
|     if kind \== "stat": p\["options"\] \= {"colorMode": "background", "graphMode": "area", "reduceOptions": {"calcs": \["lastNotNull"\]}} |
|     if kind \== "timeseries" and th: p\["fieldConfig"\]\["defaults"\]\["custom"\] \= {"thresholdsStyle": {"mode": "line+area"}} |
|     if extra: p.update(extra) |
|     return p |
| def row(pid, title, y): |
|     return {"id": pid, "type": "row", "title": title, "collapsed": False, "gridPos": {"x": 0, "y": y, "w": 24, "h": 1}, "panels": \[\]} |
|  |
| LAT\_TH \= thresholds(("green", None), ("orange", 0.5), ("red", 1)) |
| ERR\_TH \= thresholds(("green", None), ("orange", 0.01), ("red", 0.05)) |
| SAT\_TH \= thresholds(("green", None), ("orange", 0.7), ("red", 0.9)) |
| P95 \= f'histogram\_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate({BKT}{{{SEL}}}\[\$\_\_rate\_interval\])))' |
| RPS \= f'sum(rate({REQ}{{{SEL}}}\[\$\_\_rate\_interval\]))' |
| ERR \= f'(sum(rate({REQ}{{{SEL},status=\~"5.."}}\[\$\_\_rate\_interval\])) or vector(0)) / {RPS}' |
|  |
| golden \= { |
|     "uid": "shop-golden", "title": "Shop — Golden Signals", "tags": \["shop", "L3-service", "golden-signals"\], |
|     "description": "L3 service view: latency, traffic, errors and saturation of ONE service. Pick the service at the top.", |
|     "time": {"from": "now-30m", "to": "now"}, "refresh": "30s", "schemaVersion": 41, |
|     "links": \[{"title": "Up: Shop Operations", "type": "dashboards", "tags": \["L2-operations"\], "asDropdown": False, "includeVars": True, "keepTime": True}, |
|               {"title": "Runbook: checkout", "type": "link", "url": "http\://localhost:9095/runbooks/RB-CHK-002.html", "targetBlank": True}\], |
|     "templating": {"list": \[ |
|         {"name": "env", "label": "Environment", "type": "custom", "query": "lab,prod", "current": {"text": "lab", "value": "lab"}}, |
|         {"name": "service", "label": "Service", "type": "query", "datasource": DS, "refresh": 2, "sort": 1, |
|          "query": {"query": f'label\_values({REQ}{{env="\$env"}}, service)', "refId": "service"}, |
|          "definition": f'label\_values({REQ}{{env="\$env"}}, service)', "current": {"text": "checkout", "value": "checkout"}}, |
|         {"name": "route", "label": "Route", "type": "query", "datasource": DS, "refresh": 2, "includeAll": True, "multi": True, "allValue": ".\*", |
|          "query": {"query": f'label\_values({REQ}{{env="\$env",service="\$service"}}, route)', "refId": "route"}, |
|          "definition": f'label\_values({REQ}{{env="\$env",service="\$service"}}, route)', "current": {"text": "All", "value": "\$\_\_all"}}, |
|     \]}, |
|     "panels": \[ |
|         row(1, "Golden signals — \$service (now)", 0), |
|         panel(2, "stat", "Latency p95", "95 % of requests to \$service were faster than this. Orange \> 0.5 s, red \> 1 s.", 0, 1, 6, 4, \[P95\], "s", LAT\_TH), |
|         panel(3, "stat", "Traffic", "Requests per second handled by \$service.", 6, 1, 6, 4, \[RPS\], "reqps"), |
|         panel(4, "stat", "Errors (5xx %)", "Share of requests answered with HTTP 5xx. Orange \> 1 %, red \> 5 %.", 12, 1, 6, 4, \[ERR\], "percentunit", ERR\_TH), |
|         panel(5, "text", "Saturation — build me", "Placeholder for the saturation stat (Task 2).", 18, 1, 6, 4, \[\], "none", |
|               extra={"options": {"mode": "markdown", "content": "\*\*Task 2:\*\* replace this panel with a \*Saturation\* stat (CPU of \`\$service\`)."}, "targets": \[\]}), |
|         row(6, "Latency & traffic — trends", 5), |
|         panel(7, "timeseries", "Latency p50 / p95 / p99", "Percentiles of request duration. A gap between p50 and p99 means a slow minority.", 0, 6, 12, 8, |
|               \[f'histogram\_quantile({q}, sum by (le) (rate({BKT}{{{SEL}}}\[\$\_\_rate\_interval\])))' for q in ("0.5", "0.95", "0.99")\], "s", LAT\_TH, \["p50", "p95", "p99"\]), |
|         panel(8, "timeseries", "Traffic by route", "Requests per second per route of \$service.", 12, 6, 12, 8, |
|               \[f'sum by (route) (rate({REQ}{{{SEL}}}\[\$\_\_rate\_interval\]))'\], "reqps", legend=\["{{route}}"\]), |
|         row(9, "Errors — trends", 14), |
|         panel(10, "timeseries", "Error ratio (5xx)", "Share of 5xx responses over time.", 0, 15, 12, 8, \[ERR\], "percentunit", ERR\_TH, \["5xx ratio"\]), |
|         panel(11, "timeseries", "Non-2xx responses by status", "Which status codes are returned, per second.", 12, 15, 12, 8, |
|               \[f'sum by (status) (rate({REQ}{{{SEL},status\!\~"2.."}}\[\$\_\_rate\_interval\]))'\], "reqps", legend=\["{{status}}"\]), |
|     \], |
| } |
|  |
| E \= 'env="\$env",service="frontend"' |
| AVAIL \= f'1 \- (sum(increase({REQ}{{{E},status=\~"5.."}}\[\$\_\_range\])) or vector(0)) / sum(increase({REQ}{{{E}}}\[\$\_\_range\]))' |
| executive \= { |
|     "uid": "shop-exec", "title": "Shop — Executive Summary", "tags": \["shop", "L1-executive"\], |

|     \], |
| } |

| **2.A  During db-pool the checkout service is red for latency and errors but green for saturation. What does that tell you, and where would you look next?**  : **Answer:** It indicates that CPU is not the bottleneck—the checkout service is spending its time waiting on an external dependency (specifically exhausted database connections) rather than performing heavy CPU processing. Next, I would check the **L2 Operational Dashboard** (Shop Operations) to inspect **DB pool utilisation and pending threads** as well as downstream services (payment), or drill down into **L4 Explore (traces and logs)** for checkout to see where requests are stalling or failing.  |
| **2.B  Why is one dashboard with a service variable better than one copy per service?**  : **Answer:** Using a single parameterized dashboard with a service variable eliminates duplication and maintenance drift—any layout fix, threshold update, or new panel applies automatically to every service without editing multiple copies. It also enforces a consistent layout and signal order across all services and enables clean drill-down links (includeVars) from L2 to L3 during an incident.   |

Which changes improved the score most, and which finding is still open?**  : **Answer:** The new audit score improves to **16–17 / 18** (up from 7–8 / 18). The changes that improved the score most were fixing the default env variable to lab, reordering the top row to the standard Golden Signal sequence (**Latency → Traffic → Errors → Saturation**), setting an on-call time range (now-1h) with 30s auto-refresh, adding descriptions and units, and adding Up/Down hierarchy and runbook links. | **3.B  Why did you copy the dashboard instead of editing Shop Overview, and how would you make the change permanent in a real team?**  : **Answer:** Shop Overview is a **provisioned dashboard** managed by configuration files—editing it directly risks either failing to save or having our changes overwritten whenever Grafana restarts or re-provisions, and copying preserves a safe baseline while testing. In a real team, we would make the change permanent using **Dashboards-as-Code**: export the updated JSON model, commit it to a Git repository, and deploy it via CI/CD or Grafana provisioning / Terraform.   |

| **4.A  The fault made checkout red on L2/L3, but L1 stays green for the hour. Is that correct design? What would turn L1 red?**  : **Answer:** Yes, that is correct design. L1 (Executive) measures overall business-level SLOs and availability across a longer time window (such as 1 hour or days), so a brief 2-minute fault on a single internal service consumes part of the error budget (\~50–60% left) without breaching the overall hourly availability target (\~99.7–99.8%). L1 would turn **red** if the fault lasted long enough (or affected enough customer traffic) to exhaust the error budget, drop overall availability below the SLO target, or push end-to-end checkout p95 latency above the **1 s** executive threshold.  |
| **4.B  Shop Operations is missing from the tag=shop search. Fix it and explain why tags matter for the hierarchy links.** : **Answer:** Adding the shop tag to Shop Operations includes it in the tag=shop hierarchy search alongside L1 and L3. Tags matter because Grafana's **Dashboards-type links** (such as *"Down: Shop Operations"* or *"Down: Golden Signals"*) dynamically discover and populate target dashboards by matching tags rather than hardcoding URLs—ensuring the L1 → L2 → L3 navigation links work automatically and preserve the active time range and variables.   |

# 6\. TROUBLESHOOTING — COMMON ISSUES & FIXES

| Issue / Error | Cause | Diagnosis | Fix |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Docker pull fails or hangs | No internet access, registry limit or proxy | docker compose pull shows the failing image | Retry on another network; ask the instructor for the offline image bundle |
| 401 Unauthorized from the API | Wrong Grafana password in \$G | \$G/health works, /api/search does not | Use GRAFANA\_PASSWORD from .env (change the .env value, then ./scripts/reset.sh) |
| "Cannot save provisioned dashboard" | Editing Shop Overview itself | Dashboard settings show "provisioned" | Save dashboard ▾ → Save as copy |
| Service drop-down empty | env not lab or no data yet | Check the env variable | Select env \= lab; wait 30 s; refresh the variable |
| Down link shows nothing | Target dashboard lacks the tag | \$G/search?tag=L3-service | Add the tag in dashboard settings |
| Saturation stat "No data" | Typo in the query or service var | Run the query in Explore | Copy the query exactly; service \= checkout |

## 7.1  Discussion Questions

| Discussion 1 — The 5-Second Test |
| :---- |
| What did you write in the Pre-Lab after 5 seconds, and what would you write now for Shop Operations? |
| Which single change helped the most? |
|  |
| Key insight: the first row and the default variables decide whether a dashboard can be scanned. |
| **Discussion 2 — Symptom vs Cause** |
| Why did the checkout Golden Signals show latency and errors but no saturation? |
| How should an L3 dashboard point to dependencies? |
|  |
| Key answer: golden signals of a service show its symptoms; the cause (inventory DB pool) is found in its dependency — add dependency links or panels. |
| **Discussion 3 — Executive View** |
| Should management see the 2-minute fault on L1? Why or why not? |
| What time range and refresh fit an executive dashboard? |
|  |
| Answer: L1 summarises against objectives over longer periods; short incidents show as consumed error budget, not as red tiles. |
| **Discussion 4 — Ownership** |
| Who owns each of the three dashboards, and how are changes reviewed? |
| How would you keep them as code (provisioning, Git, dashboards.py)? |
|  |
| Key answer: each dashboard has an owner; JSON in Git with provisioning or the API prevents drift and undocumented edits. |

## 7.2  Common Mistakes — Learn From These

| Mistake | Why It Happens | Consequence | Prevention |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Every graph on one page | Adding is easy | Unreadable during incidents | One audience per dashboard; hierarchy |
| Answer at the bottom | Order of creation | Fails 5-second test | Summary stats in the first row |
| Numbers without units | Defaults kept | Misread values | Set unit and thresholds on every panel |
| Copy per service | Quick start | Drift between copies | Service variable |
| No links | Not thought of | Responders get lost | Up/Down links with includeVars and keepTime |

"percentunit" }\] }           \]         }       }     \]   \| { dashboard: .dashboard, folderUid: "shop-l3", overwrite: true } ' \> /tmp/shop-golden-ext-b.json \$G/dashboards/db \-d @/tmp/shop-golden-ext-b  |
| **Extension C — Dashboards as Code** |
| Change dashboards.py to add the saturation stat and re-publish. |
| Compare the generated JSON with your UI-built panel. |
| Which approach would you use for 50 services? **Answer:** **Yes.** When investigating a failing entry-point service (such as frontend), the responder immediately sees the request rate and 5xx error ratio of every downstream dependency (checkout, payment) in the same view and can pivot directly to the failing service's Golden Signals in **one click** via the data link—without having to navigate back up to L2 or manually switch the service dropdown.  |

# 10\. QUICK REFERENCE — DASHBOARD DESIGN COMMAND CARD

Bookmark this page. Every command you need in SOP order.

| Category | Command | Purpose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Golden signals | Latency · Traffic · Errors · Saturation | Same order everywhere |
| Hierarchy | L1 Executive → L2 Operations → L3 Service → Explore | Drill down |
| First row | 4–6 stats with units and thresholds | 5-second test |
| Service variable | label\_values(metric{env="\$env"}, service) | One dashboard, many services |
| Chained variable | label\_values(metric{service="\$service"}, route) | Dependent filter |
| Saturation | max(process\_cpu\_utilization\_ratio{service="\$service"}) | Percent (0.0-1.0) |
| Error ratio | (sum(rate(x{status=\~"5.."}\[\$\_\_rate\_interval\])) or vector(0)) / sum(rate(x\[…\])) | percentunit |
| Executive range | increase(x\[\$\_\_range\]) | Whole time range |
| Availability | 1 \- errors / requests over \$\_\_range | vs objective |
| Error budget | 1 \- (1 \- availability) / (1 \- objective) | Remaining |
| Links | Type Dashboards, tags, includeVars, keepTime | Navigation |
| Publish via API | POST /api/dashboards/db {dashboard, folderUid, overwrite} | As code |

# APPENDIX A — INSTRUCTOR PRE-CLASS RUNBOOK (INSTRUCTOR ONLY)

INSTRUCTOR ONLY — this lab needs no cloud account and no other lab. Each learner runs the kit on their own laptop (Docker Desktop or Docker Engine with Compose v2) or on a personal VM (2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM is plenty for one learner; about 600 MB RAM and 1.5 GB disk per stack).  
1\. Distribute lab4-kit.zip (or the folder) one day before. Learners with limited bandwidth pull the images once: prom/prometheus:v3.5.0, grafana/grafana:12.0.2, python:3.12-slim (about 900 MB in total). For a locked-down network, export the images with docker save and share the tar file.  
2\. The kit binds all ports to 127.0.0.1. For a VM that learners reach from a browser, set BIND=0.0.0.0 in .env and open 3000, 9090 and 9095 only to the learner's own IP; the Grafana password in .env is a placeholder that must be changed.

| ⌨  Instructor — kit self-test (run once before class) |
| :---- |
|  |
| \# 1\. Start and verify (all lines OK) |
| cd \~/day5-lab4 && ./scripts/setup.sh |
| \# 2\. Rehearse the fault: p95 of checkout ≈ 2.4 s and errors ≈ 35 % after about 90 seconds; then switch it off |
| ./scripts/fault.sh db-pool; sleep 120; ./scripts/fault.sh none |
| \# 3\. Back to the starting state between rehearsals or after a failed learner run |
| ./scripts/reset.sh |

3\. Platform notes: Grafana 12 and the dashboard JSON schema (schemaVersion 41\) were written against Grafana 12.0.x; if you change the image tag, import golden-signals.json and executive.json once to check them. Expected values in this guide (≈ 8 req/s, p95 ≈ 0.24 s, CPU ≈ 30 %) come from ShopSim and can differ by a few per cent on slow machines.  
4\. Clean-up: docker compose down \-v removes the containers and volumes; delete the folder to remove the kit. Nothing else is installed on the learner machine.
